title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan Jaffe, Sandra Jaffe Interview, 1961-11-25
interviewee: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan Jaffe, Sandra Jaffe

blocks.x: How old were you when you started playing?
About 18.
Had you ever played any instrument before that?
No, well I was just playing by air.
And let's talk, they've started the tape running, okay? Do you mind telling me how old you are?
Go back to the time you started, you're such a famous band leader, but...

Well, when I started running, I guess I was about 15 or 16 years old when I first started, you know, playing the trumpet, you know what I mean? Just learning how to play, you know? When I did learn, I learned about two, three numbers, I used to go play all night.
With just the two, three numbers?
Yeah, all night I used to play the same number over and over, play slow one time, next time fast.
How did you get a job with it?

Oh, we used to get a lot of work. People, them days, them days wasn't like people today, you know? Anything you do, if you take a tin pan and hit on that dance, you see? But them days, you know what I mean, that's how it was, you see? So, well, we, after that, when we began, me, Edmund Hall, Robert Hall, we all organized a little band, you see? We got a band together, then we began to play, you know, out in the country where I'm from, reserve, you see? So we played for this fella, putting here three or four nights a week, you know what I mean, like that, you know? And so, well, we couldn't play no more than three or four numbers, than a couple numbers, you see? Just play them over and over. So, well, after that, well, we just continued, continued, continued, continued. Then we began to get real good, you see? So what we did, we bought a clarinet for Robert Hall, the oldest brother. So his brother, Edmund Hall, he learned on the clarinet. They all learned on the same clarinet, you see? So, well, we began to really get good. So after what we did, we got a fella that bought a set of instruments. Brand new set of instruments at Royal Iron. And then after that, we began to get real famous then, you see? So we used to play for a fella here at the pavilion out there. And so, and the fella had their druggers. He put up a medicine. He had put up a medicine and he wanted us to name our band after that medicine. Niles Band, you see?
And you did name it that then?

Niles Band. So after that, well, we bring it, we bring it real good, you see? So we've been going all over and playing, you know what I mean? Playing all around, you see? So Edmund, he left. My cousin, Nile Thomas, he left and went to Baton Rouge. And so I got the other brother, Clarence Hall, he played with me. He played the banjo with us. So he left. So I was the last one to leave. You see, to come here, you see? Yeah. So, well, finally, well, I was the last one. So after they all left, I played with the band on the other side of the river, up in, way up there in Vachery. I played with the band there. I used to play with that band. So, well, that band was a good band, too. We were famous, too. We used to go all over and travel everywhere, all over.
Mr. Thomas, wait a minute. I want to take you back a little bit. You said you were 15 when you started playing the trumpet.
Oh, I don't know about that.
Who gave you the money to buy the trumpet? Did you earn it?

No, my daddy. You see, my daddy, he used to play in the brass band. And he used to have rehearsal there, you know, at the house sometimes. But, you know, we used to go from house to house. Well, they would leave all the instruments there. Well, we all decided what instruments we would like to learn. See, first, I used to play with the trumpet, play the trombone, and all, you know what I mean? The sliding trombone and the key trombone, you know what I mean? So, well, a fella, another boy was playing with us. Well, he died. The drum player, he died, him. Boy, another boy was playing with us. Well, he's still living. He live out there. Trombone player, you see? Well, he's still living out there, you see? So, well, after that, well, after everybody, we all, everybody got good, so everybody started to leave. See, so I was the last one to leave while I played with that band out there, you see? So, I played with that band a long time, you know what I mean? The fellas didn't even want me to leave, you see? So, well, finally I came down here, and I came down and played with a fella. He was a, he had a, he had a trumpet player playing with him, but the man died. On, he died. Connelly and Ramport came from playing in Kenner. He drank some of that old bad, overnight liquor, and killed him. He was sitting right on his case, waiting for the call.
No kidding, he died like that?

He died right there. So, this boy, his brother-in-law told him, he said, I know a fella you might get to play with you. He said, live out there in the country. He said, why don't you write to him? So, he write, he written to me, but I was already down here already, see? So, I went on over there, and LJ is on the other side. I went over there, so, we got together with the little band. And, well, then, fellas, you know, they was already playing. See, they had the band, it was just the trumpet player they needed, you see? So, well, finally, well, we went on and got together. Well, we wouldn't do no playing, we wouldn't take no engagement, we just rehearsed. We rehearsed three or four times a week. We could get a lot of weight, but we just wouldn't take it, we just wouldn't get everything straight. So, well, after that, the first job I played, Joe, it was for the, you know, pavilion. It rained all day and all night. No kidding. Yeah, all day and all night. The first game game, we played for white people. And after that, lady, we start sailing. I used to have so much weight that sometime I wouldn't put my shoe off a whole week.
Well, weren't you terribly tired? How'd you get any rest?

Well, I just, well, I, you see, when I would get my rest, I'd take a good one, you see? I really take a good one. So, after that, well, we started going all over. Play on the lake. The lakefront was open, you see? You have picnics and things. We play excursions, known for the railroad. And different things, like different picnics, kind of, you know, picnics, you know, like that. Like the holiday, like that. We play picnics all over. We play everywhere, you know what I mean? I played in all, I played in the Blue Room. I played in the Blue Room. I played in Mont Leon Hotel. I played in all them hotels.
Well, Mr. Thomas, how, how, you said when you first started you could play only three songs. How did you gradually get from there to the point where you could learn more?

Well, I just kept, I just kept playing. I take one song at a time. Well, who'd teach it to you? Did you just listen? Nobody. We had no teacher. What'd you do? Did you sit down and try to figure it out alone? I just, just listen to other, probably just whistle numbers and we just play them.
Would he whistle a tune to you and you? Yeah, yeah, yeah, that's how, that's how we used to do.
Well, how did you ever learn to use your lips right? Well, I just practiced. That's all.
Well, then having a father that played instruments helped though, didn't it?
That's right. But you see, he didn't play no trumpet, you see?
What, what do you think about you taking up the trumpet? Oh, he liked it, that.
My grandfather didn't approve of it at all. Why? Oh, no, he religious.
I couldn't even play my horn around the house. Well, now why, I thought, I thought this music had such a part in religion. Why didn't?
No, no, he didn't like that. My grandfather, my grandma, they didn't like music.
What did they say when you were playing?

I used to leave and go play my, go in them halls in different places, go to other people's houses and go on. It didn't stop me at all. I just kept, I just continued going, you know what I mean? So, when I found myself, well, I was down here.
Well, do you think that this revival of jazz is a good thing now?
Sure. And you see, I tell later, I never did, I never changed my style of playing. I would just play the same way and my same style, never changed.
But it's a great style.
Oh, yes, ma'am. That's right.
Thank you, sir. That's right.
Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Oh, you have the drawing.
Where did the name jazz start?

No, that's another thing a lot of people have been talking and arguing about for years. Actually, it seems the name jazz has applied to the music, wasn't used with the music until it got to Chicago, probably, as far as we know. Although sometimes you'll find people down here that'll claim they maybe heard the word used in connection with music and somebody will dig it up as being used, oh, way back, oh, 50 years before anybody ever heard of a jazz band and all of that. But to me, the name has never been important. I never even think about it. Most of the music, older musicians here will call it ragtime. They'll talk about the ragtime bands and they just think of it as the music, the dance music that they played.
Well, how did this all start? Does it really have a unique start here in New Orleans?

To me, as far as I've been able to discover, I think the type of music that we call jazz today and this American dance music, what might be called the hotter variety, the more improvised form of it, as far as I've been able to determine, it really did start here.
Most of these musicians don't know how to read music, though, do they?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I'd say probably at least half of them have. Even the best ones. If you, all the way back to the 1890s even. Probably more of them in the beginning knew how to read music than some of the musicians today.
Well, these bands that started here in New Orleans, how did they start?

Well, there's a lot of theories on it that came from the parade music and came from blues or from some of the work songs. Actually, a lot of it is European. And there's this big argument about the African influence on it, which is difficult to prove. There was definitely an African strain in it, though, as far as I've been able to discover, too. Certain elements there that I've never come across in ordinary European music.
Well, the rhythm is so much stronger than European music, isn't it?

Maybe, but not necessarily. There have been some strong, like, look at the Spanish music. Yeah. And some of that was influenced by African music, too. Well, this also... The Cuban type of music. It's all very rhythmic.
Well, this rhythmic element is basic to what we now call jazz, though, isn't it?

Oh, yes. It's one of the main things, is the definite rhythm to it, the definite beat that it has, and a certain kind of, not necessarily just simple syncopation, as they usually used to talk about, but there's just a certain kind of a swing to it. They never have found really a good term to express it, but once you hear it, I mean, you get that feeling, a foot-tapping feeling, and a certain happy feeling about the beat that goes on and on.
Well, what about the harmonic structure? I mean, how is this...

Well, the harmony, in general, down here was always simplified. That's why some people think the musicians were uneducated, but not necessarily. But they, as a rule, they would simplify rather than develop. The harmony didn't seem to be as important as the melody and the rhythm, those two elements. Usually, European music is considered as having melody, rhythm, and harmony. But the melody and the rhythm, I'd say, are the two main factors that you can distinguish New Orleans music. They always stick to the melody. They always have a melody going. Yeah. It isn't like bop or some other music that just has just plain rhythm like a lot of... Sometimes they do riffing and all here, too, but some forms of jazz, it has very little melody. You just get on a little phrase or on a certain little motive and repeat it over and over again. Well, that could be a melody, too. But, I mean, here, they usually like to have a regular tune, something that the people can actually hear and whistle and hum, you know.
Well, how important was the religious feeling in influencing all of this? Well, I think that's difficult to say, too.

Of course, for people like me that came down here years after it started, I would never know. But other people like, say, Kid Ori, for instance, and some of the first people I met in California, like Bud Scott, one of the old-timers, quite a few of those said that a lot of the music came right out of the churches of the jazz bands as if... I know it was either Ori or Bud Scott. I don't remember which one. It could have been Mutt Carey. I'm talking about Buddy Bolden. They said, well, he got all of his music right out of the Baptist church. He used to take his girlfriend whom he later married with, either Nora or Dora Bass. There were two twins. In fact, he took them both to church. He said he came out of that church and began swinging as if it were that simple. Of course, nothing could be quite that simple, but the churches always have had that wonderful beat in their music and a good melody and all going to... Maybe not so much harmony as we understand it, but they still have it. That church music has changed evidently very little, even compared to the jazz.
What about the street marches, the funeral marches? Are they all the same thing?

In a way, that might have influenced jazz too, but I don't know. I would be hesitant to say that it actually had as great an influence as other things. Maybe the jazz influenced the street marches more than the other way around. Although, the fact that they were marches and had that definite beat in a lot of the marches are used as dance pieces. Well, of course, the obvious one is high society and a few others have been too. But, one thing you might notice in the street marches, which has relation to jazz, is the slower tempo. If you watch the high school bands here and especially other parts of the country down here too, now they go so fast you have to run with it to keep up with them. But the old time colored bands and the old time white bands too, as far as that goes, in general, just an old time New Orleans band on the street, goes along in keeping with the hot climate that we have. They don't like to hurry. They take their time. They really... And they do that in the jazz too. Any time you hear a real fast tempo, you can be sure that had nothing to do with the original New Orleans jazz. Because even things like Tiger Rag and those tunes, they didn't race them. They didn't, as they call it today, race horse music. They didn't do any of that. As far as we know, the old time New Orleans musicians. It was always a more relaxed feeling and slower. And that, of course, could have come from the slower marches, just in general, the slower tempo of life in the hot climate.
Well, was there much difference, or is there to this day much difference between the all Negro jazz band and the all white jazz band?

Oh, it's hard to say. There won't be much longer, if there is any now. There wouldn't be much longer. Because the Negroes, of course, get all of their music from television and radio and records, and it all comes through New York and Hollywood, probably, today. And it's all going to end up exactly the same.
Well, what about this pure jazz that all of you are trying to preserve?

Well, there may be a little difference, a little difference in the feeling of the white and the colored. It's hard to put your finger on it, though, and say definitely, because some of the white musicians undoubtedly played the same style as the colored in the old days. Maybe the colored held on to that old time feeling a little bit better, a little bit longer than the white musicians. But today, they all call it, for instance, Dixieland. A lot of people try to make a big point between what they call New Orleans style and Dixieland style, which I've never been able to see, actually, any real. Just a question of terms like using jazz or ragtime. You can call it anything you want to, and it's difficult, of course. And this is one of our friends, Al Rose, is trying to get a certain definition adopted so that people wouldn't be calling everything under the sun jazz, which in a way is a good idea. Because you can get into all sorts of arguments by somebody calling one type of music jazz and really thinking it is.
Well, which came first, the colored movement towards ragtime and blues or the white movement towards ragtime and blues, or were they simultaneous?

Well, they might have been pretty close together. Even in the, for instance, in the funerals, today the only bands, the colored bands that march in the street for funerals, the only bands that march are the colored ones. But, oh, you can dig up history books and old newspaper accounts of white bands playing back maybe as early as 1850, way back in there. Oh, that's that early. And they'll talk about after the funeral, too, that they'll, maybe they didn't, it wasn't real jazz as we know it today, but at least they played lively pieces on the way back from the funeral. Uh-huh. And some of the white bands certainly did that in the 1890s at the same time that the colored bands were doing it, too. So it would be difficult to say, some people try to say, oh, that started in Italy or someplace, too. In fact, in New York, they still, the Italian section, at least 30 years ago when I was around, they, the Italians used brass bands for their funerals, too. And the Chinese used different sorts of bands, I don't know, I did hear one once in San Francisco, but never got close enough to it to really study just what they were doing.

Well, as, as the music moved out of New Orleans, was there a distinct change when it got to Chicago, for example, or when it got to Kansas City, or when it moved on to the West Coast? Did it lose some of its flavor, or did it add something? How did that work?

Oh, undoubtedly the different environment would change anything, but I think the New Orleans musicians probably played very similar. I mean, it's a question of the individual, but to me, it would seem to be more important. A fellow wouldn't change his style just because he went to Chicago suddenly. In time, if he had to play with some of the different musicians, Chicago musicians that weren't used to his style, he would change and he'd lose certain part of his style, his certain beat that he had maybe, or different things. But in general, the bands that would leave here, with mostly New Orleans musicians, undoubtedly, must have played very similar. Other people will try to claim that they actually heard him. I wasn't here to hear the difference between, say, the Oliver Band, the way they played here, and when they got to Chicago.
But some people claim they are different.

Some people didn't. Like Dr. Sushon, for instance, who heard them up there and had heard them down here, and a few other people, have claimed that there was some difference already as soon as they got up there.
Well, Mr. Russell, what are you doing now at Tulane in this sort of research project towards preservation of jazz?

Well, it's strictly a collection project at present. We're collecting interviews, trying to preserve all that history of the old. The older the musicians, the better, of course, and other people, too, that happen to hear the music or maybe help promote it. In some cases, the wives and the daughters, sometimes the women know more about the history of it than the men, because maybe the husband went to work every night and played in one band, and the wife might have gotten around the different dances and heard different bands. Occasionally, they have a better memory, too. So it isn't just the musicians that we're interviewing.
But this, this, excuse me, go ahead.

Yes, but almost anyone who would remember some of the music back, oh, especially 40 to 60 years ago, those are the people we're trying to interview and collect the tape interviews. Also, we collect the phonograph records, which didn't come in until roughly 1917 on, especially through the 20s. So by that time, some of the music might have been sort of corrupted, some people might think, and we don't know, actually, because we don't have the old examples on record.
Well, was there a difference in the style in Storyville, the so-called body house area?

Well, some people make a big point about the jazz originating in Storyville, which is hardly possible, because it must have been pretty well formed before, well, Storyville itself, the term wasn't used until after, about 1897 when they set these certain legal districts. The district had been there long before that, though. But they never had employed bands so much. They mostly employed piano players until, oh, maybe say around the 1910 period when more instrumental music became popular there. And more, there always were a few dance halls probably there, but the cabarets and dance halls mostly opened up in that period between 1910 and 1920, probably.
Well, it was a jazz band for dancing then, wasn't it? Not just listening.

Oh, yes. It was just for listening. It never was for listening, probably, in the old days. It was either for dancing. Of course, they used the jazz bands for every possible kind of a party, like, say, a christening or a birthday party or almost any kind of a party that anyone would ever have. They would always have a band in the old days. And they advertised at prize fights, at the prize fight, between rounds or before the fight started. They would, any kind of an athletic event, they would use on boats, on excursions. Oh, they're just, that's what everybody talks about, that there was music all over the city. Just any place you went, you'd hear a jazz band playing in the old days.
Well, it is dying out, though, isn't it?

In that respect, it is. Since the jukeboxes, I don't know what it would be, whether it's the radio or jukeboxes or phonograph records or just what exactly killed it, but, well, even Kid Thomas, who's playing across the street, other people have used the same expression, exactly the same expression, that the city's like a cemetery, like a graveyard today, compared to how lively it was, say, 30 to 50 years ago that they remember.
Well, then maybe radio had a direct influence in cutting down some of it.

It could have had some influence, undoubtedly. And the, now every corner saloon has a jukebox. In the old days, especially on weekends, at least they would have had a jazz band. And anybody that had a party, a christening or a wedding party or a birthday, any kind of a party at all that you'd give, not just New Year's and the big holidays, but any kind of a party, they'd have, they'd be sure to hire a jazz band, maybe only three or four pieces, but, or if nothing else, maybe a piano player. They had fish fries every, it was an institution every Friday, I think, was the main day for fish fries. They'd have lawn parties, just dozens of things. You could probably couldn't go but a few blocks, but you'd run into some sort of music in the old days.
Well, what can be done to preserve this? I mean, there's no way to teach it.

Well, there's no way to, you'd have to change the whole country and change the whole environment, undoubtedly. I've never made any social studies of just what's happening, but I mean, the world does change. Maybe it doesn't progress, but at least it sure changes. And in the changing process, the jazz has just fallen by the wayside somewhere.
But it's typically American.

Oh yes, it seemed to be something definitely developed in America, and I'm ready to believe from what I've seen and heard, that most of the better bands did originate here. Right in New Orleans. Right in New Orleans. There's been just entirely too many musicians here to say that, well, it's probably just the ones you heard of here. The ones that became famous happened to be born here, but there were so many here compared to other cities. There was nothing to compare with them in the north where I was raised, in other towns. I didn't have the experience of being all over the country, and maybe even early enough to hear the bands, what was happening in New York. But judging from the phonograph records and other things that we'd been able to pin down, there was nothing up there that had the real jazz element in it in the beginning. Thank you.

How'd you get the idea to come down here and start this New Orleans revival of jazz or work with it? Well, we didn't come down here for that specific purpose. We came down from Philadelphia in about April and thought we'd be hearing a lot of these musicians and a lot of this music. And we didn't. We knew a lot of these men were still alive, that bands like the Eureka and Young Tuxedo Brass bands were still organized, and they were not playing anywhere. The first time that we saw them was about a month later. We saw Eureka hats and instruments walking down the street, so we followed them to the museum on Jackson Square, the Cabildo. And there the Eureka played for the Friends of the Cabildo, which was a humorous sight. All the Dowagers and friends and people sitting there. And the first few blasts of the horns, I thought the ceiling would fall in and the floor would open and the paintings of all the portraits of the ancestors would come off the walls. But they had the crowd swinging after a while. Well, so, but you must have known something about jazz. Well, Alan was a big jazz fan, and I knew a little bit about it, but I wasn't that involved in Philadelphia. But I did like it very much, and I did expect to hear a lot of it down here. But at this time, I had no sort of attachment to any of these men. I knew nothing about their status down here or anything about their not playing down here. And once coming down here, I became more sympathetic to the situation, which eventually evolved in our starting across the street. Well, Alan, let me ask you how you found these men. I mean, you didn't just wander freely around and say, do you play an instrument?

Well, really, when we started, there was a group of people involved in this person we rent from now, Larry Bornstein, had been running these sessions on an informal basis. That would be, I guess, for at least 10 years. The band would come in occasionally during the night when they weren't playing. He'd open up his gallery to them and pass the kitty and pay them in from that. Mr. Russell had been down here for quite a while doing research on the musicians. And a boy here from California by the name of Grayson Mills who did a lot of initial work in getting the musicians started. Once the men started playing and a lot of other men started finding a way around to us, still there are a lot of people we would like to get to play for us that haven't been around. The only way we really know about the men are still around are through people like Mr. Russell and people who do come around.
How did you get hold of these men in the first place? Did they find out about you?
Well, these men are, you know, live here. Yeah. And a lot of them are quite famous. People like Jim Robinson, George Lewis, Kit Howard, I mean...
Excuse me for interrupting you here, Alan, but you said George Lewis. Now Lewis has just returned from Europe. How do you get him to come back here and play a one-night or a two-night stand?

George is happy to. George likes to play. He likes to be heard. He's happy to play with any band who he can work with. And I mean by working with, I mean, this is people who he can produce the type of music with that he wants to.

Well, did you find that you sort of got hold of a lot of extra musicians by word of mouth? Did they sort of come from the woods? Did they? Yes. Yes. I think we started out with just a few bands. In fact, when it first began, they were rotating a band once a week. And that's come to the point where we have over 20 bands and over 160 musicians that are just all seem to be falling into place. The orchestras and the bands are being more organized. At one time, a lot of the personnel were interchanging and taking their place with other leaders. But now, there is not very much of that unless a man happens to be away. Well, how do you get the bands? Do you organize the bands or do they organize themselves? No, they're organizing themselves. We've been hiring the leaders.

What we do is hire a person who is a leader, who had been a leader in the past. This is a person who is a leader musically and who knows the sound that he wants to produce from a band. He knows the other musicians and we hire a man, tell him to bring six pieces and he brings five musicians. Sometimes they're people we haven't heard before. A lot of times they're people we have heard before.

Were you able to discern which bands are better than others? I mean, do you sort of say to someone, thank you, we don't want you anymore? We haven't had to. In other words, they're all of a pretty good quality then.

Well, each band, as my wife said, there are 20 and each one is different. It's, the quality is certainly different. And I think the musical idea that the people are trying to get across is different also. There's range from Peter Boccage who plays a more subdued, a more quiet type music, quiet for jazz anyway. Maybe a little more sophisticated than a person, a kid Thomas. Yeah. Where a kid Thomas is, is a lot, maybe rougher, a lot more direct.
Well, Alan, do you, this music is very exciting music and do you ever have any trouble with the crowds pushing in, with the crowds creating a riot, anything like this? Sort of.

We have, by, you know, simply arranging seats, we sort of build a barrier to keep the people away from the musicians. And the people who are in front of me actually are sitting on the floor, they can't stand. And we haven't had too much of a problem of people actually, you know, rushing up to the band. We've had times when it's taking the band five minutes to get off the stand and get back to get a break. But that's what we're doing.
How, how strong is the union in, in, in setting prices, here's salaries, in setting times for them to play, this sort of thing?

We've been fortunate, the president of the union happens to be a very fine musician who plays here quite frequently. In fact, Lewis Gattrell's band will be playing tomorrow night. Uh, even very cooperative. We adhere to all union regulations, we pay them on union scale, and work union hours.

But there's something interesting that you do over here, it's sort of hard to describe. You, you don't charge anything to get in, but you sort of pass the kitty. Can, can you actually make enough on this to pay the musicians? What about it, Sandra? Sometimes. Um, Saturday nights we usually do. And on Friday nights, well, the past two weeks have been rather slow, but our first two months here we've been able to meet expenses. Um, we thought about charging an admission, but there are a lot of problems involved once we do that. And we're going to be waiting a while and see how the unorthodox procedure of our business goes. If it goes alright and if we're able to meet expenses, we're going to keep it at kitty contributions. Well now, both of you are holding down outside jobs, and this means that you work normal hours from 9 to 5, and then you come down here starting at 8.30 and run until 12.30, right?
That's right.
Well doesn't this get a little complicated, Alan? How can you, how can you manage a, a life of your own? And, aside from this, the actual working hours, it's, it's the coordinating.
It's not really complicated at all, you just, you just forget about your private life.
You throw it out the window? Yes. Well do you feel as if you're, uh, sort of crusading?

It's a silly question. No, not really. What do people do? It's funny that, uh, I think both of us feel, you know, quite privileged that we're able to be able to do this. The musicians are fine people, they're people who it's really an honor to be associated with. And, to be able to do what we're doing, even though it's long hours and we're not paying ourselves any salaries, and not really making anything, in fact, at times costing us something, other than just our time, uh, it's still just a thrill to hear these men play, to, to hear a new musician, to hear people improve from playing frequently.

Have you seen the crowds grow since, since you first started? Oh yes, and, uh, also we've noticed that we're getting a steady clientele of people, uh, people that are living in the city, that are coming back, and people from out of town who have heard by word of mouth. It's growing. We have... Yes. A lot of people... Not too many people from Birmingham, though.

We have a lot of people here who now know that this is going, people throughout the country, throughout the world, as a matter of fact, who are, who are interested in hearing this music, are now coming in. People from California...
Yes, Canada, all over.
We hope to have a whole tour of people from France next year coming here.
Just to hear this.
Just to hear this.
Thank you.

Uh, I better leave a tail on it. Thank you. There's a lot more I wanted to ask you, but I thought that this would probably suffice for what I'm doing. Uh, first of all, it's, it's Alan and Sandra Jaffe, right? And I've got your address. And, uh, this, this, I, so is it any, I, I, you just call it preservation... You just call it preservation... ... ... ...

segments.title: Fragment: starting at about 18, playing by ear
segments.summary: A short fragment of another interview: the speaker began at about 18 with no earlier instrument, playing by ear.

segments.title: Kid Thomas learns trumpet and forms the Niles Band with the Halls
segments.summary: Kid Thomas is 65; he began trumpet at 15-16, played all night on a few numbers, organized a band with Edmond and Robert Hall, got instruments, and named it after a medicine.

segments.title: His father's brass band, and coming to New Orleans to replace a dead trumpeter
segments.summary: His father bought the trumpet and the family band rehearsed at home; he later left for the city to join a band whose trumpeter had died of bad liquor.

segments.title: Heavy work schedule: picnics, excursions, hotels
segments.summary: After the first pavilion job he worked constantly, playing the lakefront, railroad excursions, picnics, the Blue Room and hotels.

segments.title: Learning by ear with no teacher
segments.summary: He learned song by song, by listening and whistling, with no teacher, and practiced his lip himself.

segments.title: Religious grandparents disapproved of his music
segments.summary: His father played in a brass band but not trumpet; his religious grandparents disliked music, so he played in halls and at other people's houses.

segments.title: The jazz revival and never changing his style
segments.summary: He approves of the revival and says he has never changed his style.

segments.title: Bill Russell on the word jazz, its New Orleans origin and reading music
segments.summary: Russell says the name jazz came in Chicago, older musicians said ragtime, the music started in New Orleans, and many early players read music.

segments.title: Origins of the bands: European and African elements, rhythm
segments.summary: Russell discusses theories of origin, African versus European influence, and the swing and beat at the heart of the music.

segments.title: Simple harmony, melody and rhythm in New Orleans music
segments.summary: Harmony was simplified; melody and rhythm distinguish New Orleans music, unlike bop.

segments.title: Church music and Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: California old-timers like Ory and Bud Scott said the music came from church; Bolden supposedly took his music from the Baptist church.

segments.title: Street marches and the slow New Orleans tempo
segments.summary: Marches may have influenced jazz mainly through their slow tempo, suited to the hot climate; fast tempos are not original.

segments.title: White and Black bands, Dixieland terms and early funeral bands
segments.summary: Russell discusses differences between white and Black bands, the Dixieland label, Al Rose's definition, and early white funeral bands.

segments.title: Did the music change in Chicago? The Oliver band
segments.summary: Russell thinks musicians kept their style; Dr. Souchon claimed a difference once the Oliver band reached Chicago.

segments.title: The Tulane collection project: interviews and records
segments.summary: Russell describes collecting interviews with musicians, wives and listeners, and phonograph records.

segments.title: Storyville and jazz bands for dancing and every occasion
segments.summary: Jazz did not originate in Storyville, which employed bands mainly after about 1910; bands played for parties, fights and excursions.

segments.title: Why the music is dying out: jukeboxes and a changed city
segments.summary: The city is now like a graveyard compared to earlier; jukeboxes and radio replaced bands at parties and saloons.

segments.title: Jazz as American, with the best bands from New Orleans
segments.summary: Russell argues that jazz developed in America and that most of the better bands originated in New Orleans.

segments.title: Sandra Jaffe on coming from Philadelphia and seeing the Eureka band
segments.summary: The Jaffes came from Philadelphia expecting to hear the music, found the bands idle, and followed the Eureka to the Cabildo.

segments.title: How the hall found its musicians
segments.summary: Allan Jaffe describes the earlier informal sessions in the landlord's gallery, Russell's and Grayson Mills's help, and getting George Lewis to play.

segments.title: Twenty bands, hiring leaders, and differences among them
segments.summary: They hire leaders who bring their own players; over 20 bands and 160 musicians; Peter Bocage is more subdued than Kid Thomas.

segments.title: Crowd control and union scale
segments.summary: Seating barriers manage crowds, and the hall follows union scale and hours with a cooperative union president.

segments.title: Passing the kitty and the Jaffes' double lives
segments.summary: No admission, only a kitty; they hold day jobs, work long hours unpaid, and feel privileged.

segments.title: Growing crowds and visitors from around the world
segments.summary: A steady clientele and out-of-town visitors are growing; a tour from France is expected.

segments.title: Closing the tape
segments.summary: Hanson thanks them, notes the tape tail and confirms the Jaffes' details.
